title: Rounded box by offset of an exact box (r < min(b)/2)
description: rounded_box[r,b] = offset r << box.exact(b - 2*r). The offset trick is the implicit equivalent of a constant-radius fillet on every edge at once.

parameters.name: radius
parameters.description: corner radius = offset distance

parameters.name: box_size
parameters.description: edge length of the exact box before offset

code:
let
    rounded_box[r, b :: is_vec3] = offset r << box.exact(b - 2*r);
in
union [
    rounded_box[.5, [2,2,2]],
    cube 2 >> translate[3,0,0],
]

constraints.why: box.exact(b-2*r) goes non-positive at r = b/2, so the offset has nothing to round
at equality the result is a sphere

nomination.reason: one offset replaces N edge fillets and cannot fail on tangency the way fillet-by-edge does; Atta has no offset-based rounding path

title: NewVoxelSDF3(sdf, meshCells) — voxelise a deep field to flatten evaluation cost
description: Samples a deep SDF3 hierarchy into a voxel grid and evaluates against that, trading exactness for a bounded per-sample cost. This is the practical answer to 'implicit models get slow'.

parameters.name: meshCells
parameters.description: grid resolution per axis; cost is O(meshCells^3) memory

parameters.name: progress
parameters.description: progress channel (chan float64) — plumbing, not geometry

constraints.why: below 16 the cached field loses the feature; 2048^3 floats is ~32GB
voxel caching rounds detail smaller than a cell — a finish decision, not an accident

title: expand({delta, corners, segments}) — round/edge/chamfer expansion of 2D and 3D
description: The offset-family op with an explicit corner rule and a segment budget: this is the finish op that turns a sharp outline into a rounded one without a fillet kernel.

parameters.name: delta
parameters.description: expansion distance; negative shrinks

parameters.name: corners
parameters.description: corner treatment during expansion

parameters.name: segments
parameters.description: segments per rounded corner — the resolution knob

parameters.name: arc_radius
parameters.description: radius of the demo arc being expanded

parameters.name: arc_end_angle
parameters.description: end angle of the demo arc (PI/2)

constraints.why: expanding further than half the narrowest feature closes slots and merges islands (offset self-intersection)

nomination.reason: a single op with a corners enum replaces fillet/chamfer/shell for most finish work, and it degrades gracefully

title: roundedCuboid with an explicit corner-radius parameter
description: The primitive every CAD library ends up needing: a box with one radius for all edges. Its declared parameter block is a ready-made Atta param schema.

parameters.name: width
parameters.description: x extent

parameters.name: height
parameters.description: y extent

parameters.name: depth
parameters.description: z extent

parameters.name: radius
parameters.description: corner radius

parameters.name: rounded
parameters.description: 0 = sharp, 1 = rounded

constraints.why: radius above half the smallest edge degenerates the box into a capsule/sphere and the flat faces vanish

title: Blind hole as a first-class b-rep feature (face + position + depth)
description: add_blind_hole(HoleLocation{face, position}, radius, [0,0,depth]): the hole is addressed by face and 2D position, not by subtracting a cylinder. That is the feature-ordering lesson: name the face, then place the feature on it.

parameters.name: radius
parameters.description: hole radius

parameters.name: depth
parameters.description: blind depth = size/2 in the source

parameters.name: size
parameters.description: body size derived as radius*4

parameters.name: face_index
parameters.description: index of the target face (source uses nth(5) = bottom)

constraints.why: a blind hole deeper than the body becomes a through hole and silently changes genus
very shallow blind holes are a degenerate boolean (coplanar bottom face)

nomination.reason: face-relative hole placement (face id + 2D position) is how a b-rep kernel avoids the coplanar-boolean class of failures; Atta's hole op is origin-relative only

title: Dual-offset fillet: offset(r=-k) after offset(delta=+k) rounds concave corners
description: The manual gives the two canonical offset idioms. Fillet (inside corners): offset(r=-3) then offset(delta=+3) rounds every concave corner and leaves flat walls untouched. Round (outside corners): offset(r=+3) then offset(delta=-3) rounds every convex corner and leaves flat walls untouched. r rotates a circle of that radius about the outline (rounded corners); delta moves the outline and therefore keeps angled corners.

parameters.name: r
parameters.description: radius of the circle rolled around the outline (default parameter; offset(c) == offset(r=c))

parameters.name: delta
parameters.description: distance of the new outline from the original; reproduces angled corners

parameters.name: chamfer
parameters.description: with delta: cut corners with a straight line instead of extending to their intersection; no effect on radial offsets

parameters.name: fn
parameters.description: $fn — circle resolution; affects radial offsets only

constraints.why: manual, explicit: with the fillet idiom 'holes less than 2*r in diameter vanish'
manual, explicit: with the round idiom 'walls less than 2*r thick vanish'
delta offsets generate no inward perimeter where the perimeter would cross itself — self-intersection is clipped, not repaired

nomination.reason: a dual offset rounds every edge of a solid in two ops, with no edge selection and no tangency failure mode — the single most portable finish trick in the corpus

notes: Paraphrase of the WIkibooks OpenSCAD manual 'Transformations' page, offset section. Both idioms are given verbatim in the page as 'Fillet:' and 'Round:'.

title: offset() parameter semantics: r (radial) vs delta (outline distance) vs chamfer
description: r and delta are not interchangeable: r rolls a circle and yields rounded corners, delta translates the outline and yields angled corners. chamfer only applies to delta and swaps the corner extension for a straight cut. $fa/$fs/$fn control smoothness for radial offsets only ('they have no effect on delta offsets').

parameters.name: r
parameters.description: radial offset radius (default param)

parameters.name: delta
parameters.description: outline offset distance; sign selects in/out

parameters.name: chamfer
parameters.description: delta only: straight corner cut

parameters.name: fa
parameters.description: $fa — minimum angle per fragment

parameters.name: fs
parameters.description: $fs — minimum fragment size

parameters.name: fn
parameters.description: $fn — fixed fragment count; 0 means 'derive from $fa/$fs'

constraints.why: the manual states chamfer has no effect on radial offsets
$fa/$fs/$fn have no effect on delta offsets — a resolution knob that silently does nothing

notes: Paraphrase of the same page's parameter list; the two 'no effect' statements are the load-bearing part and are quoted as constraints, not copied as text.

title: $fa / $fs / $fn — the three-way resolution contract
description: Faceting is a first-class design parameter in CSG systems. $fn fixes the fragment count (0 = auto), $fa sets the minimum angle per fragment and $fs the minimum fragment length; $fn wins when non-zero. The same trio governs extrusion slices, radial offsets and glyph subdivision, so a part's cost and its silhouette are set by three numbers.

parameters.name: fn
parameters.description: fixed fragments; 0 = auto

parameters.name: fa
parameters.description: minimum angle per fragment (coarse floor)

parameters.name: fs
parameters.description: minimum fragment size (fine floor)

constraints.expr: fn == 0 or (fa is ignored and fs is ignored)
constraints.why: a non-zero $fn overrides $fa/$fs entirely — setting all three is a common source of 'my smoothness knob did nothing'
fragment count drives mesh size superlinearly once the shape is revolved or swept

title: hull() — convex hull as the cheap bridge/transition op
description: hull() returns the convex hull of its children, and the page notes that for convex polygons fill() is identical to hull(). It is the standard way to build a transition between two sections without a real loft kernel.

parameters.name: convexity
parameters.description: preview hint for how many front faces a ray can cross; the manual calls 10 'a good value to try'

constraints.why: a hull cannot reproduce a concave transition — concave features between the two children are filled in

title: Blender Bevel modifier: width types, limit methods, profile, miters
description: The most complete public statement of bevel semantics. Width can be interpreted as Offset, Width or Percent of the adjacent edge length; Limit Method restricts the bevel to Angle-similar or weighted edges; Profile interpolates the cross-section from concave to convex and is inert when Segments < 2; miters resolve where two beveled edges meet, with separate inner/outer patterns.

parameters.name: width
parameters.description: bevel size; interpretation depends on width_type

parameters.name: width_type
parameters.description: how width is interpreted (Offset / Width / Percent of edge length)

parameters.name: segments
parameters.description: cross-section resolution; profile has no effect below 2

parameters.name: profile
parameters.description: cross-section shape, concave (0) to convex (1); inert at segments<2

parameters.name: limit_method
parameters.description: which edges are beveled

parameters.name: angle_limit
parameters.description: with limit_method=ANGLE: only edges sharper than this are beveled

constraints.why: manual: profile 'has no effect if Segments is less than 2'
a bevel wider than half the shortest adjacent edge consumes the edge and neighbouring bevels collide (clamp overlap)
the Angle method bevels edges whose adjacent face-normal angle plus the limit is below 180 deg — the intended reading is 'sharp edges only'

nomination.reason: width_type + limit_method + profile is a far better finish schema than a bare 'fillet radius': it separates how much, where, and what shape

notes: Paraphrase of the Blender manual Bevel modifier page. Blender's manual is CC-BY-SA; no text is copied and no code field is written.

title: CadQuery selectors: features are applied to *selected topology*, not coordinates
description: CadQuery's fluent API chains operations on a Workplane, and the load-bearing idea is the selector: faces('>Z'), vertices(), edges('|Z') pick topology by direction and then the next call (circle, cutThruAll, extrude, fillet) applies to that selection. This is how a code-CAD system avoids re-specifying coordinates for every subsequent feature.

parameters.name: selector
parameters.description: topology selector string: '>Z' max-Z face, '|Z' edges parallel to Z, '#Z' etc.

parameters.name: radius
parameters.description: fillet radius applied to the selected edge set

parameters.name: thickness
parameters.description: distance used by extrude/cutThruAll on the selected face

constraints.why: an empty selection silently no-ops in a fluent chain — the classic silent-failure mode of selector-based CAD
the fillet must fit the adjacent edge or the kernel either fails or eats the neighbouring face

nomination.reason: Atta's ops take coordinates; a selector op would let a feature say 'fillet the edges parallel to Z' and survive a parameter change

notes: Paraphrase of the CadQuery primer (Apache-2.0 project; the docs page is fetched from readthedocs). The selector concept is illustrated by the primer's own chain box -> faces('>Z') -> vertices -> circle -> cutThruAll.

title: Minkowski sum with a star-shaped tool (the smoothed-offset workaround)
description: Builds a 'star' by unioning hulls of a tiny cube translated in 6 axis directions, subtracts a sphere from a cube, then takes the Minkowski sum. Because manifold has no general Minkowski sum, the example approximates it with a convex tool.

parameters.name: probe_size
parameters.description: small cube edge used to build the tool

parameters.name: probe_offset
parameters.description: axis offset of each hull probe

parameters.name: sphere_radius
parameters.description: sphere subtracted from the cube

parameters.name: sphere_segments
parameters.description: sphere facet count

parameters.name: cube_size
parameters.description: base cube edge

code:
import numpy as np
from manifold3d import Manifold


def run():
    small_cube = Manifold.cube([0.1, 0.1, 0.1], True)
    cube_vertices = small_cube.to_mesh().vert_properties[:, :3]
    star = Manifold.as_original(small_cube)
    for offset in [
        [[0.2, 0.0, 0.0]],
        [[-0.2, 0.0, 0.0]],
        [[0.0, 0.2, 0.0]],
        [[0.0, -0.2, 0.0]],
        [[0.0, 0.0, 0.2]],
        [[0.0, 0.0, -0.2]],
    ]:
        star += Manifold.hull_points(np.concatenate((cube_vertices, offset), axis=0))

    sphere = Manifold.sphere(0.6, 15)
    cube = Manifold.cube([1.0, 1.0, 1.0], True)
    sphereless_cube = cube - sphere
    return sphereless_cube.minkowski_sum(star)

constraints.why: the hull-based construction only yields a valid Minkowski tool when the tool is convex; a concave tool needs a real sum
probes further apart than the body produce disconnected offsets

title: Scalloped smoothing by assigning tangents to half-edges
description: Manual smoothing: rather than subdividing, the example assigns tangents to each half-edge and lets the interpolator produce a scalloped surface. A height/radius pair plus per-edge tangents is the whole control surface.

parameters.name: height
parameters.description: shell height of the scalloped form

parameters.name: radius
parameters.description: base radius

parameters.name: rings
parameters.description: ring count around the form

parameters.name: tangent_scale
parameters.description: magnitude of the assigned half-edge tangents (smoothing strength)

from manifold3d import Manifold, Mesh
import numpy as np


def run():
    # A smoothed manifold demonstrating manual smoothing by assigning tangents to
    # halfedges. Use refine() before export to see the curvature.

    height = 10
    radius = 30
    offset = 20
    wiggles = 12
    lean = 0.3
    frontal_sharpness = 1
    n = 50

    def lerp(a, b, t):
        return np.array(a) + (np.array(b) - np.array(a)) * t

    triangles = []
    positions = [[-offset, 0, height], [-offset, 0, -height]]
    halfedge_tangent = []

    len_ = np.pi * radius / (2 * wiggles)
    top_normal = np.array([-lean, 0, np.sqrt(1 - lean * lean)])
    delta = np.pi / wiggles
    center_tangents = [None] * (2 * wiggles)
    edge_tangents = [None] * (2 * wiggles)

    for i in range(2 * wiggles):
        theta = i * delta
        amp = 0.5 * height * (np.cos(theta) + 1) / 2
        v = np.array(
            [
                radius * np.cos(theta),
                radius * np.sin(theta),
                amp * (1 if i % 2 == 0 else -1),
            ],
            dtype=np.float64,
        )

        positions.append(v.tolist())

        center_tan = np.array([(v[0] + offset) / 2, v[1] / 2, (v[2] - height) / 2])
        center_tangents[i] = center_tan - np.dot(center_tan, top_normal) * top_normal
        edge_tangents[i] = np.array([-len_ * np.sin(theta), len_ * np.cos(theta), 0.0])

    for i in range(2 * wiggles):
        next_i = 0 if i + 1 == 2 * wiggles else i + 1

        radial = center_tangents[i]
        next_radial = center_tangents[next_i]
        edge = edge_tangents[i]
        next_edge = -edge_tangents[next_i]
        sharpness = frontal_sharpness * (np.cos(i * delta) + 1) / 4
        up = lerp(
            np.array([0, 0, len_]),
            np.array([next_edge[1], -next_edge[0], 0]),
            sharpness,
        )
        down = lerp(
            np.array([0, 0, -len_]), np.array([-edge[1], edge[0], 0]), sharpness
        )

        triangles.append([0, 2 + i, 2 + next_i])
// …excerpt truncated…

constraints.why: zero tangents collapse the scallop back to a faceted lathe
too many rings for the height creates sub-facet scallops that disappear after meshing

title: libfive rounded_rectangle(a, b, r) — 2D rounded rect as a first-class field
description: One signature for the 2D rounded rectangle: two bounds and one radius. Because it is a field, the corners are exactly circular at any scale (no chord error), which is the property a mesh kernel cannot promise.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: first corner (vec2)

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: opposite corner (vec2)

parameters.name: r
parameters.description: corner radius

constraints.why: a radius above half the shorter side leaves no straight edge and the rounded rect degenerates to a stadium/circle

title: libfive rounded_box(a, b, r) — 3D rounded box in one call
description: The 3D sibling of rounded_rectangle: bounds plus radius, all twelve edges rounded at once. Compare the Curv idiom offset(r) << box.exact(b-2r) — same maths, one op versus two.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: min corner (vec3)

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: max corner (vec3)

parameters.name: r
parameters.description: edge/corner radius

constraints.why: at r = half the smallest extent the box becomes a capsule, beyond it the box.exact core goes non-positive

title: Manifold's contract: guaranteed manifold output 'without caveats or edge cases'
description: Manifold states its primary goal as reliability — guaranteed manifold output with no edge cases — and defines a manifold mesh as one that represents a solid object. That is a *verifiable* contract: closed surface, every edge shared by exactly two half-edges, consistent orientation. It is the property Atta's verify gate should assert directly rather than infer from volume.

parameters.name: min_volume
parameters.description: volume floor; a manifold result of ~0 volume is a degenerate solid

parameters.name: max_genus
parameters.description: genus bound; booleans that unintentionally add tunnels break it

parameters.name: epsilon
parameters.description: geometric tolerance below which vertices are merged

constraints.why: the definition of manifoldness the README relies on; a boundary edge means the solid is not a solid
flipped normals make a valid mesh render and slice wrongly

nomination.reason: Atta verify should assert manifoldness directly (edge-face incidence, orientation) instead of inferring it from volume/genus windows

notes: Paraphrase of the Manifold README's stated goal. Manifold is Apache-2.0 (Tier A) but this record is a docs record: it carries the contract, not code.

title: difference() is order-sensitive: 'and not', first child is the minuend
description: The manual states the three CSG ops propositionally — union = or, difference = and not, intersection = and — and demonstrates that swapping children of difference() gives the complement of the intent (square minus circle versus circle minus square). union and intersection are commutative; difference is not.

parameters.name: operand_count
parameters.description: children; for difference every child after the first is subtracted

parameters.name: order_sensitive
parameters.description: difference only; union/intersection are commutative

parameters.name: convexity
parameters.description: preview front-face crossing hint for the boolean result

constraints.why: manual: difference is 'and not'; the first child is the body and every later child removes material — reversing them yields the complement
only difference carries an order dependency, so a reordering pass may only touch union/intersection nodes

title: convexity is a rendering hint, not geometry — and its absence looks like a bug
description: convexity tells the preview how many front faces a ray can cross, so it controls how many faces OpenSCAD may cull. It does not change geometry; it changes whether parts of the model appear transparent. The extrusion page adds the practical rule: if an extrusion looks wrong, 10 is the value to try, and the default is not 10.

parameters.name: convexity
parameters.description: front-face crossing count; 10 is the documented 'good value to try'

parameters.name: render_path
parameters.description: preview uses the hint; a full render evaluates the real CSG tree

constraints.why: a convexity fix changes the picture, never the solid — do not accept it as a geometry fix in review
manual: 'the default is not 10, but 10 is a good value to try'

title: box_exact vs box_mitered: two incompatible conventions for 'a box' in a field
description: libfive ships two boxes and says so in the names. box_exact(a,b) is the true Euclidean box field (corners are exact points, so offsets round them). box_mitered(a,b) is the mitered variant whose field is cheaper and whose offsets give sharp/mitred corners. The choice changes what every downstream offset, shell and fillet does.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: min corner (vec3)

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: max corner (vec3)

parameters.name: variant
parameters.description: exact = Euclidean box (rounds under offset); mitered = mitred corners

constraints.why: offsetting a mitered box gives mitred, not rounded, corners — the finish op inherits the box convention

constraints.expr: all boxes in a tree use one variant
constraints.why: mixing conventions makes offsets behave differently per part in one assembly

nomination.reason: Atta has one box primitive; the exact/mitered split is why offset rounding behaves inconsistently between tools
